subtitle: Informal notes on discussions with Steve Crocker about the proposed NCP protocol

tldr.problem: The Meyer proposal (RFC 46) and Crocker's comments raise seven key issues about the socket-based NCP protocol that need debate and consensus.
tldr.mechanism: Meyer documents positions taken in telephone conversations: dynamic reconnection should wait, INT command is useful, socket identifiers need instance tags, data should have no imposed structure, and a standard User Control and Communication protocol is essential for network-wide compatibility.
tldr.outcome: These discussions reveal fundamental design tradeoffs in early ARPANET protocol development, balancing simplicity against functionality and standardization against flexibility.

today: RFC 49 documents a critical moment in ARPANET protocol design when the community had to choose between competing philosophies. Meyer's insistence on a standard UCC protocol proved prescient; the Internet's success depended on such standards.

sections.title: Discussion Topics
sections.content: Meyer documents telephone conversations with Steve Crocker at UCLA on April 21 and 23, 1970, concerning the Meyer proposal in RFC 46. The discussions cover seven significant protocol design issues: dynamic reconnection, the INT interrupt command, socket identifiers and instance tags, data structure at the NCP level, character sets and echoing, request queuing strategies, and the User Control and Communication (UCC) protocol for login. Each issue represents a tradeoff between simplicity and functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Meyer writes down what he and Crocker discussed about how to design the network protocol, covering seven important choices.

sections.title: Points of Agreement
sections.content: Meyer and Crocker agree on several fundamentals: dynamic reconnection should be reserved for future implementation (it would over-complicate the initial protocol), the INT command is valuable for interrupting processes, no structure should be imposed on data at the NCP level (leaving character set questions for higher protocols), and a standard UCC protocol is absolutely essential. Meyer emphasizes that without a standard UCC implemented at all sites, installations will create separate incompatible protocols, fragmenting the network. This disagreement with Crocker highlights a fundamental insight: standardization, even if imperfect, is more valuable than flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: They agree that keeping the basic protocol simple is important, that the login protocol must be standard everywhere, and that higher-level protocols should decide how data looks.

sections.title: Unresolved Issues
sections.content: Meyer remains undecided on whether socket identifiers should include instance tags (separate fields that distinguish multiple processes of the same user). Crocker argues that instance tags add complexity and are hard to discover. Meyer sees them as necessary but acknowledges the complexity costs. The RFC also documents security concerns about process identity: Meyer argues strongly that no process should use another user's socket codes, as this creates security breaches. The UCC protocol design itself had competing approaches: Meyer's dual full-duplex connection method versus Crocker's use of reserved sockets for login. These unresolved debates shaped the next round of protocol development.
sections.plainLanguage: They disagree about whether computer programs should be able to identify themselves separately (instance tags), and about the best way to let a new user log in to a remote computer.
